causalMechanism.primaryVector: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) cause orgasmic dysfunction primarily through serotonergic modulation of the neural circuits governing sexual response. Increased synaptic serotonin at 5-HT2 and related receptors inhibits the mesolimbic dopaminergic reward pathway and the medial preoptic area that mediate sexual desire, arousal, and the orgasmic reflex; serotonergic effects on the spinal ejaculation generator and on genital sensory processing increase the latency to orgasm and can abolish it entirely, while prolactin elevation and altered nitric-oxide-mediated genital vasocongestion contribute to impaired arousal. Orgasmic dysfunction is the most serotonergic-specific of the sexual side effects and typically appears shortly after drug initiation or dose escalation, persists for the duration of treatment, and resolves after discontinuation (the emerging literature on post-SSRI sexual dysfunction describes a subset with persisting symptoms after drug cessation). The evidence is quantitative and of high certainty: a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials in adults with depression found SSRI use significantly increased the risk of orgasmic dysfunction (RR 3.28, 95% CI 2.33-4.60, I2 = 8%, high certainty) and reduced sexual satisfaction (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.11-1.32); a prospective multicenter study of 1,022 outpatients with previously normal sexual function found an overall sexual-dysfunction incidence of 59.1%, ranging from 57.7% (fluoxetine) to 72.7% (citalopram) among SSRIs, with orgasm among the assessed domains; and a management review documents that SSRIs can cause all types of sexual side effects (libido, arousal, orgasm, and ejaculation) and that up to 80% of patients may report sexual side effects, in a class prescribed for major depressive disorder, PTSD, panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so anorgasmia developing on documented SSRI therapy for service-connected major depressive disorder (or PTSD) is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where orgasmic dysfunction predated the medication, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the SSRI agent, dose, start date, and any dose changes with the chronology of orgasmic symptoms relative to initiation; the pre-treatment sexual history and baseline function (ideally documented contemporaneously); the effect on the relationship and distress; and address competing causes — depression itself (which independently reduces sexual function), relationship and psychosocial factors, age and menopause or hypogonadism, diabetes and other neuropathy, pelvic surgery or radiation, alcohol and other drugs, and concomitant medications (other serotonergic agents, antipsychotics, beta blockers, opioids). A trial of dose reduction, switching, or augmentation is helpful evidence where medically appropriate, and the rating proceeds by analogy under § 4.20 because no diagnostic code specifically addresses orgasmic disorder.

Primary condition: Major depressive disorder (service-connected), on SSRI therapy
Primary diagnostic-code proposal: 9434 (38 CFR § 4.130 — major depressive disorder; PTSD under DC 9411 and the other SSRI-treated anxiety and trauma disorders follow the same treatment pathway)
Secondary condition: Anorgasmia (orgasmic dysfunction)
Secondary diagnostic-code proposal: No dedicated DC — evaluated by analogy under 38 CFR § 4.20 to the disability picture, within the § 4.115b genitourinary framework (erectile dysfunction, DC 7522, is the closest content-matched schedule entry for the male analog); § 4.116 applies where the presentation is gynecological in character
Original nexus theory: Medication Side Effect
CFR citations (preserved in order):
[
  "38 CFR § 3.310(a) (disability proximately due to or the result of a service-connected disease or injury, including its treatment)",
  "38 CFR § 3.310(b) (aggravation of a nonservice-connected disability, with baseline rule)",
  "38 CFR § 4.130, DC 9434 (major depressive disorder) and DC 9411 (posttraumatic stress disorder)",
  "38 CFR § 4.20 (analogous rating of unlisted orgasmic disorder within the § 4.115b framework; DC 7522 for the male analog) and § 4.116 where gynecological in character"
]

Legal boundary: § 3.310(a) concerns proximate causation; § 3.310(b) concerns attributable worsening beyond natural progression against a qualifying baseline. The at least as likely as not standard requires individual evidence and competing causes to be weighed. Apply claim-period rating criteria and § 4.14 nonpyramiding.
